title: The Next Mythos Moments
gist: After Anthropic's Mythos cyber model triggered three US policy reversals in two months — a voluntary pre-release-sharing executive order, a worldwide ban on Mythos plus a block on OpenAI's latest model, then a lifting of both — two Carnegie fellows argue the next capability jumps will be in biology, open-source releases and compute scarcity, all with longer lead times or outright irreversibility, and urge building CAISI evaluation capacity and allied compute buildouts before the next crisis forces a crackdown.

insights.claim: Anthropic announced a powerful new cybersecurity model called Mythos in April 2026, and major companies with early access warned it could undermine the security of critical U.S. infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht, Alasdair Phillips-Robins
insights.so_what: Establishes that a single model release can trigger national-security-grade policy response — a discrete regulatory event risk for frontier labs.
insights.locator: The Trump administration appears to be struggling

insights.claim: The Trump administration reversed AI policy three times in under two months: an early-June executive order creating a voluntary pre-release model-sharing process, then within two weeks a worldwide ban on access to Mythos plus a bar on public release of OpenAI's latest model, then a lifting of both restrictions at the end of June.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht, Alasdair Phillips-Robins
insights.so_what: Regulatory whiplash of this speed makes deployment timing an unhedgeable risk for AI product roadmaps and for capital committed to model launches.
insights.locator: Less than two weeks later, the Trump administration switched course again

insights.claim: The government shut down public access to Mythos entirely in response to a vulnerability that Anthropic claimed was common across many openly available models, showing how a generic flaw can produce a single-vendor ban.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht, Alasdair Phillips-Robins
insights.so_what: Enforcement can land arbitrarily on the most visible vendor rather than the actual risk distribution — idiosyncratic company-level risk.
insights.locator: And before long, the government had shut down public access

insights.claim: Reporting on frequent personality clashes between Anthropic and the U.S. government suggests that passing a discretionary pre-deployment review could depend on government relations at least as much as on substantive safety standards.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht, Alasdair Phillips-Robins
insights.so_what: Political-relationship quality becomes a competitive variable between frontier labs — a soft moat and a soft risk.
insights.locator: Based on reporting on frequent personality clashes

insights.claim: Just as training models as software engineers produced emergent advanced cybersecurity capability, advances in AI for biological research — a top goal of the leading labs — will likely let criminals, non-state actors and U.S. adversaries design chemical and biological weapons.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht, Alasdair Phillips-Robins
insights.so_what: Bio capability is the next policy trigger — AI-for-biology investments carry a regulatory cliff that cyber-focused models have already demonstrated.
insights.locator: First, biological threats

insights.claim: The clearance threshold for releasing an open-source model may be prohibitively high because attackers can remove built-in safeguards after release, whereas proprietary models can be vetted partly on those safeguards.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht, Alasdair Phillips-Robins
insights.so_what: Implies a structurally different — and far harsher — regulatory regime for open weights than for API-gated models.
insights.locator: Second, dangerous capabilities will once again raise questions

insights.claim: When the White House stalled the rollout of Mythos to a wider range of firms, officials cited compute constraints as one important reason, meaning compute scarcity is already shaping deployment policy rather than being a purely commercial issue.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht, Alasdair Phillips-Robins
insights.so_what: Non-obvious: compute allocation has become a policy lever, so government demand can crowd out commercial inference capacity.
insights.locator: Finally, rising demand for AI is pushing the world into a compute crunch

insights.claim: If compute remains scarce once AI becomes essential to U.S. military and intelligence services, policymakers may come to regret the sale of advanced chips to China and other nonallied countries.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht, Alasdair Phillips-Robins
insights.so_what: A national-security compute squeeze is the mechanism that would retroactively tighten chip export policy — a downside scenario for China-exposed semi revenue.
insights.locator: Today, the chip shortage is mostly a commercial concern

insights.claim: The triggering events for sudden AI policy shifts could be a single highly capable new model release or a Taiwan conflict that shuts off chip supplies.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht, Alasdair Phillips-Robins
insights.so_what: Two discrete, monitorable catalysts that would convert gradual AI policy into emergency intervention.
insights.locator: Those risks could arise suddenly

insights.claim: Mythos was comparatively easy to manage because defenders in control of important software, including Mozilla and Palo Alto Networks, used a private version of the tool to identify and patch vulnerabilities before they could be exploited — a few weeks of lead time may have been all defenders needed.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht, Alasdair Phillips-Robins
insights.so_what: Privileged early access to offensive AI is emerging as a defensive product category — a new revenue and moat line for security vendors.
insights.locator: What's more, Mythos was, in some ways, easy to deal with

insights.claim: Risk classes differ by reversibility: cyber vulnerabilities can be patched within weeks, biological responses such as vaccines, resilient infrastructure and stockpiles have long lead times, and open-model deployment and chip exports are effectively irreversible once done.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht, Alasdair Phillips-Robins
insights.so_what: A clean triage framework for AI risk: irreversible categories justify pre-emptive restriction, which is where policy will tighten first.
insights.locator: And both open-source deployments and compute exports share an element of irreversibility

insights.claim: Building societal resilience to biological weapons after developing the models that accelerate them is not feasible, since perfect pathogen resilience is costly, time intensive and nearly impossible compared with cyber resilience.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht, Alasdair Phillips-Robins
insights.so_what: Implies pre-deployment approval alone cannot handle bio risk — expect demand for synthesis screening, pathogen surveillance and stockpiling capacity.
insights.locator: If the private-sector response to Mythos works

insights.claim: Frontier labs have floated the possibility of a coordinated slowdown in AI development while acknowledging that none of them can individually reach such an outcome.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht, Alasdair Phillips-Robins
insights.so_what: A textbook collective-action failure: no unilateral slowdown will occur, so capability escalation continues absent state coordination.
insights.locator: No wonder, then, that frontier labs have floated

insights.claim: Kevin Hassett, director of the White House National Economic Council, called for an FDA-style oversight model requiring AI models to be proved safe before release in the same way new drugs and vaccines must pass safety trials.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht, Alasdair Phillips-Robins
insights.so_what: An FDA-for-AI proposal from inside the NEC is the most severe realistic regulatory scenario — it would gate revenue timing for every frontier lab.
insights.locator: Kevin Hassett, the director of the White House National Economic Council

insights.claim: If civilian agencies cannot respond to AI-driven threats, intelligence and military agencies become the default AI regulator despite their bias toward secrecy and centralized control, difficulty adapting to commercially developed technology, and historically limited role in domestic regulation.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht, Alasdair Phillips-Robins
insights.so_what: Securitized AI regulation means opaque decisions with little industry recourse — a governance risk that is worse for open-weight and startup players than for incumbents.
insights.locator: For one, intelligence agencies or the military could emerge

insights.claim: A plausible scenario is a Mythos-style ban applied to open-source models developed in the U.S. or even merely deployed on U.S. servers, with evaluations conducted in secret and few pathways for civil society or industry to challenge them.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht, Alasdair Phillips-Robins
insights.so_what: US-hosted open-weight distribution and inference businesses carry a specific, underpriced ban scenario.
insights.locator: It is easy to imagine a Mythos-like ban applied

insights.claim: Ad hoc AI policy produces governance by streetlight, in which whatever the administration happens to become aware of gets regulated while whatever developers successfully conceal remains unregulated.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht, Alasdair Phillips-Robins
insights.so_what: Selection bias in enforcement rewards opacity — assume voluntary disclosure regimes systematically miss the worst capabilities.
insights.quote: The risk is governance by streetlight
insights.locator: Spur-of-the-moment decisions are also more likely

insights.claim: Without a mechanism compelling disclosure, an AI developer that spotted dangerous biological capabilities in its next model might think twice about approaching the administration, costing policymakers the window to prepare defenses.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht, Alasdair Phillips-Robins
insights.so_what: Punitive ad hoc responses actively suppress the voluntary reporting the government relies on — a self-defeating policy loop.
insights.locator: Given that precedent, if an AI developer were to spot

insights.claim: A deployment-focused regulatory approach fails to address some of the most serious future risks, which might come from internal company deployments rather than public releases.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht, Alasdair Phillips-Robins
insights.so_what: Internal-use models are the regulatory blind spot — where labs will concentrate their most capable systems.
insights.locator: more generally, a deployment-focused approach fails

insights.claim: Laissez-faire Republicans including venture capitalist megadonor Marc Andreessen and former AI Czar David Sacks dismiss most of these risks as hypotheticals pitched by ideological doomers, yet Sacks has conceded that the cyber risks posed by Mythos are more on the real side.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht, Alasdair Phillips-Robins
insights.so_what: The accelerationist bloc is already conceding on cyber — the deregulatory coalition is less solid than it appears when concrete national-security risk lands.
insights.locator: Of course, many influential Republicans do not believe

insights.claim: Every faction has a reason to want a formal pre-deployment structure: the AI industry to avoid the security state seizing regulatory control or a capricious White House process, Democrats to constrain the Trump White House, and populists on both sides who have long wanted stricter AI oversight.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht, Alasdair Phillips-Robins
insights.so_what: A durable coalition for structured AI review exists — meaningful institutional AI regulation is more likely than the current gridlock suggests.
insights.locator: So in reality, all sides of the AI policy debate

insights.claim: Discretionary licensing regimes with unknown standards, obscure rules and contested legal authority are unlikely to produce reliable safety benefits even though some form of government review will likely be necessary.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht, Alasdair Phillips-Robins
insights.so_what: Design quality, not just existence, of AI review determines whether it is a compliance tax or a genuine risk control.
insights.locator: As even pro-regulation voices point out

themes.theme: Prescriptions: CAISI, evaluations and compute siting

insights.claim: The recommended starting point for pre-deployment cyber-risk reviews is voluntary review through the Center for AI Standards and Innovation, which is both the U.S. government's deepest repository of AI expertise and its best bet for maintaining cooperative relations with frontier labs.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht, Alasdair Phillips-Robins
entities: Center for AI Standards and Innovation
insights.so_what: CAISI is the institution to watch as the de facto US AI gatekeeper — its budget and headcount are the leading indicator of review capacity.
insights.locator: When it comes to pre-deployment reviews of AI models for cyber risks

insights.claim: CAISI should expand its team and build open-source-specific evaluations now that account for the likely failure of built-in safeguards in the wild, because standards and evaluation protocols cannot be spun up at the eleventh hour.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht, Alasdair Phillips-Robins
entities: Center for AI Standards and Innovation
insights.so_what: Absent pre-built open-weight evaluation infrastructure, outright prohibition becomes the default policy response.
insights.locator: To prepare for a future when officials are spooked

insights.claim: Compute policy prescriptions include leaning on U.S. labs and major cloud providers to build the bulk of AI compute in the United States and closely allied countries, and at the coercive end barring large exports to countries — especially in Southeast Asia — where end users are likely to be Chinese developers, or capping total export volume to the nonallied world.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht, Alasdair Phillips-Robins
insights.so_what: Southeast Asian data-center buildouts serving Chinese demand are the specific export-control target to monitor.
insights.locator: Ensuring the U.S. has enough compute will also take planning

insights.claim: Critics currently argue there are enough chips to go around and that energy to power data centers has become the real bottleneck, but if chips become the limiting factor again their destination will grow far more important.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht, Alasdair Phillips-Robins
insights.so_what: The chips-versus-power bottleneck question determines whether export controls or power procurement is the binding constraint on AI capacity.
insights.locator: For now, critics argue that there are enough chips

insights.claim: Panicked compute restriction risks keeping more chips in the United States than the country has the land or power to run, alienating allies and hurting industry.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht, Alasdair Phillips-Robins
insights.so_what: Over-restriction creates stranded chip inventory — a real downside scenario for hardware demand if siting and power lag.
insights.locator: The trick here will be getting the balance right

insights.claim: Passing a major AI bill in 2026 looks unlikely, and neither government capacity nor the present third-party ecosystem is ready to conduct pre-deployment evaluations at scale.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht, Alasdair Phillips-Robins
insights.so_what: No federal AI statute in 2026 plus no evaluation capacity means the third-party AI audit market has room to build — and executive action fills the vacuum.
insights.locator: But passing a major AI bill in 2026 looks unlikely
